newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan rebels return from exile to make peace.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan rebels return from exile to make peace.

text.p: Left-wing rebel commanders, who spent years in exile while their depleted forces fought an unwinnable war at home, were returning to Guatemala on Saturday to sign an historic peace treaty ending their 36-year insurrection.

In a homecoming that has stirred both excitement and fear in Guatemala, the leaders of the National Guatemalan Revolutionary Unit (URNG) were due to fly in from Mexico where they had been negotiating with the government until just days before Sunday's peace ceremony.

Exiled in Mexico, the veteran four-man URNG high command controls 1,700 guerrilla troops in the mountains and jungle backwaters of Guatemala, where for 3-1/2 decades they have fought a cat-and-mouse war with the military.

This year, after negotiations brokered by the United Nations, heads of the four main URNG factions have travelled the international circuit for gala peace accord signing ceremonies in Mexico, Spain, Sweden and Norway.

The last step on that journey is Sunday's definitive treaty to end one of Latin America's longest-lasting and most brutal conflicts, in which 140,000 people -- mostly civilians -- died or "disappeared" at the hands of the right-wing military.
Peace will bring URNG commanders home and out into the open for the first time since the war started in 1961.
Weakened, shorn of international support, and tired of a conflict they admit they had long given up winning, the rebel leaders plan to forge a political party in peacetime.
Their fighting forces, still billeted in clandestine mountain camps, are set to trade in their guns for land, jobs and a long-awaited return to civilian political life in 1997.
Also Guatemala-bound on Saturday was Boutros Boutros-Ghali, outgoing Secretary-General of the United Nations, Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, and other international dignatories.

On Sunday, they will be joined by other heads of state from Latin America for the peace ceremony at 5 p.m. (2300 GMT), hosted by President Alvaro Arzu, who has won international acclaim for ending the war in less than 12 months in office.
In the capital, as many as 40,000 Guatemalans are expected to throng the main square outside the National Palace when the peace treaty is signed.

The business community -- once a pillar of the right that sought to crush the rebels and their supporters by any means available -- has seized on the accord, running commercials on television explaining in sugary terms what "peace" means.
They are painting the treaty as a "new dawn" for a country that badly needs to shake off its image of conflict and human rights abuse in order to attract investment.

"The reinsertion of the URNG to the constructive and productive efforts of the country cannot be anything other than welcomed by the Guatemalan private sector," the country's main business confederation CACIF said in a statement on Saturday.
But there were also concerns about the rebels' return that could not be supressed in a country where the Cold War raised enmity of the guerrillas by right-wingers to fever pitch.

Government officials said the rebel leaders -- Rolando Moran, Pablo Monsanto, Carlos Gonzalez and Jorge Rosal -- would not be allowed to carry arms. They would also be under the eye of part of the 5,000-strong army security contingent stationed in the capital to safeguard the signing ceremony.
They were due to arrive at Guatemala's international airport on a commercial flight by 5 p.m. (2300 GMT) on Saturday.
